utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, for the sake of the record, may we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Ken Scott. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Kenneth Scott for the Prosecutor. I am joined by Mr. Douglas Stringer, Mr. Vassily Poriouvaev, Mr. Roeland Bos, and our case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. As you can see, the whole lineup is here. Kresimir Krsnik as lead counsel, Christopher Meek as co-counsel, and Nika Pinter, our legal advisor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Branko Seric, the Defence counsel for Vinko Martinovic, and my co-counsel, Zelimir Par.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Martinovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain, or are you in good health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in good health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Status Conference is held by the scheduling order dated the 25th, January 2002 in accordance with Rule 65 bis. The purpose of this Status Conference is, by reviewing the status of the case, to ensure that the proceedings are not unduly delayed, and any necessary measures shall be taken to prepare the case for a fair and expeditious trial. This Trial Chamber is seized with two motions, one of which is from the Defence counsels; namely, the accused's joint suggestion concerning recess after Prosecutor's case, dated the 21st January, 2002. The other is the Prosecution's response to that motion, dated 25th January, 2002. The main items of this Status Conference are as follows: The first one is the admission of the Prosecution documents which was dealt with in the last sitting. The second one is the closing of the Prosecution case. The third one is the Rule 98 bis proceedings concerning with the motion for acquittal. The fourth one and the most important one is the status and the preparation of the Defence case. The fifth one is other issues that both parties may bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber. We have to deal with all those issues one by one. The first one is the admission of the Prosecution documents. As this Trial Chamber ordered orally during our last sitting, documents tendered with the last witness, Sir Martin, we expected a response from Defence counsel to this end by today, but up to now we haven't received any response yet. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to happily inform you that we delivered that response in writing to Laurent Wastelain approximately one hour ago, with the Registrar's office. The documents for Sir Martin Garrod, they have been given to Laurent approximately one hour ago, approximately 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask: Is that a joint submission or a separate one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a joint submission. And I would also like to tell the Trial Chamber that we filed a very brief response to the response filed by the Prosecutor regarding Presidential transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The second issue under this item is two additional binders of the documents from Zagreb Archive submitted by the Prosecution. We would like to hear the views expressed by Defence counsel concerning those two binders of documents during this Status Conference. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We, as directed by you, we will now give you our position on the five points presented regarding the documents provided to us by the Prosecution in two binders. I'll be very brief, and I think that I will just present five major points here. As we heard, the Defence received these documents, these two binders, six days before closing the Prosecution case. And as the lead counsel explained, they have been in the possession of the Prosecution for a long -- much longer period of time. Before next week [as interpreted], we were never served with these documents, and we could not obviously review them or use them, use them either in our cross-examination or -- or in any other way. Also, these documents were never tendered through any of the witnesses put forward by the Prosecution. In addition to these main reasons, which really would prejudice the Defence and our client should these documents be admitted, when we perused the documents and when we studied them, we noticed that some of the documents refer to the events following the time line in the indictment in 1994. I believe that some of them are -- go as far forward as 1995. And my learned colleague may correct me if I'm wrong, some may go as far forward as 1996. The -- Mr. Prelec could have been one of the persons who could have -- through whom these documents could have been entered, but because it was not done, our defence would be prejudiced. Our documents -- our defence did not have an opportunity to verify this document. Each of these documents is -- stand on its own. We cannot receive them in batches and then have them tendered in batches. Each of these documents speaks for itself individually. We know and -- in principle that these documents have come from the Zagreb Archive. This is the only thing that we know. We have no reason not to believe the Prosecutor when he said so, but we know nothing else about them before they were in the Zagreb Archive; they could have passed through the hands of various intelligence services, but we do not know who did what to them but we know that they were in possession of various intelligence agencies. This is the only thing that we can conclude about these Zagreb Archive documents based on what we have heard here in the courtroom, and we therefore cannot agree to the authenticity of these documents. Should these documents be admitted, which the Defence believes would be very prejudicial, the Defence would then at least ask that somebody confirm their authenticity, such as Mr. Prelec, for instance. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to present another position of the Defence. As we studied these documents in the last few days, we noticed that there were some documents in these binders that were seized from the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg in 1998. I do not want to belabour this, but in all our motions so far, we have given our submissions about the documents, and I do not want to repeat myself. Also, I do not want to repeat our position regarding the Zagreb documents because we have presented our views both orally and in writing. But in conclusion, let me say this: Should these documents be admitted, my client would be subjected to irreparable damage. And should they be admitted, they should be admitted only through a witness, and the witness should be subject to cross-examination. This is why we very vigorously oppose their introduction into evidence, and this is our position. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seric, do you have any additional point to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Vinko Martinovic also opposes the introduction of these documents. I am not going to go through all the documents. 2536 to 2856 is the sequence. I just want to add, with respect to everything that my learned friend Mr. Krsnik said, we were only to just glance through these documents. So we are not able to individually object to each of the documents that I have just mentioned. So we are unable to give you specific reasons for each individual document. But generally speaking, we oppose their tendering because, the way they were presented by the Prosecution, we believe that this was done at the last moment in a situation when the Prosecutor also said that they, themselves, were burdened with the inflow of these documents on a daily basis. So if we are to admit these, then we do not know where this is going to lead us. If we are going to admit these, then we don't know what else we can expect, and then the question arises whether this case is closed or not. And I believe this is something that we have to decide in this Status Conference. When is the Defence then going to be able to actually start preparing its Defence if we are going to have to spend so much time investigating the documents that are coming? If these documents are admitted, then we would have to go through each one of them to first confirm its authenticity, even though we believe this is the burden of the Prosecution because of the presumption of innocence. And no exhibit can be an exhibit unless it was properly introduced and tendered and unless its source and providence has been positively confirmed. As my learned friend put it, there will be a shadow of a doubt cast over all these exhibits, and we will not be able to know what is really behind it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I hear the response from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. There is no basis - there is no reasonable basis - to exclude these documents. No Rule, no Statute, no ruling of this institution or this Chamber has been violated in any way by the timing or the manner in which those exhibits were tendered. And for them to be excluded now would involve changing the Rules after the Prosecution has rested its case. We have said from the very beginning -- the Chamber will recall back the first day of trial when these issues were discussed at length, and it was made clear and never drawn into question again after that. The Defence had quite knowingly and quite intentionally never sought document discovery in this case under 66(B). They were, therefore, not entitled to a single document being tendered in Court. However, obviously, the Prosecution went far beyond that and provided most of its exhibits substantially before they were tendered in court. Many were tendered more than a year before the trial began. Most were tendered before the trial began. Others were tendered during the trial but usually - with some exceptions - usually from a month to six weeks before they were actually used in court, for example, the Presidential transcripts. They were tendered -- they were given to the Defence at least as early as the 11th of October. They were not tendered until the end of the case before Christmas. And I come back again; none of that was required. This Chamber has never issued a ruling requiring the advance disclosure of exhibits. There is no Rule that requires the advance disclosure of exhibits. There has been no prejudice to the Defence case. Where no right or Rule has been violated, there can be no prejudice. To the contrary, again and again and again, the Prosecution did and has done more than the Rules require. In this instance, these documents were provided a week before they were tendered into Court. Again, that was not required. There was no Rule or no ruling which required the Prosecution to disclose them at all before coming to the courtroom. There is one -- for counsel to say now, now going on some two weeks -- it is now going on some two weeks since they were first provided to the Defence, and for counsel to say, "We really don't know what they are still, we have only glanced at them," is not the fault of the Prosecution. In terms of the foundation that was laid for these documents, Mr. Marko Prelec came twice. Gave similar testimony, frankly, on two occasions. There is no reason, there is no good-faith basis that has been put forward to quarrel or question that these documents indeed came from the Zagreb Archive. Mr. Prelec testified twice about the Zagreb Archive. And if the Chamber really wants Mr. Prelec to come back and say exactly the same things again, that can be arranged. The timing of the -- there was a complaint about two of the documents being beyond the time of the indictment. There are two documents dated after the time of the indictment, but they specifically refer to events in 1992 and 1993. P802.1 refers to events on the 18th of September, 1993. P896 refers to various events taking place during the time between 1992 and 1993. They are not beyond the scope of the indictment in the case. In reference to documents seized, there was one document seized; one seized document on the list. All other documents came from the Zagreb Archive. Mr. Van Hecke, on the first day of trial, on the 10th of September provided extensive testimony to the Chamber about the seizure of documents. Again, that foundation was laid. Mr. President, it is obvious, I think, from my statements our firm position, there is no reasonable basis to exclude those documents, no Rule. No ruling has been violated. There has been no prejudice to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you want to reply? You have to be very concise because this issue is not the main subject of this status conference. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We must reply to the submissions of the Prosecutor. The way I have understood our oral arguments today in this hearing had to deal with these two last binders. But it seems as if we need to talk about all the other documents which have been tendered so far. I believe that this is not the right forum to revisit the issue of the documents which have been tendered before. What the Defence said is that we received those two binders on the last day of their case in chief, and we presented our position in regard of that material. If you would like to, we can talk about the other documents, too, entered through Mr. Van Hecke and Mr. Prelec. But we do not know how certain documents appeared either at Siroki Brijeg or in the Zagreb Archives. How are we to know that somebody did not deliberately draft or compile these documents in order to damage either the HVO or anyone else? So there could be forgeries. We heard no one except for the investigator, that is, a staff member here, who are partial parties, who only explained to us how those documents came into their possession. As far as the Presidential documents are concerned, I do not want to trouble you with those. But if this Chamber is to admit the documents, entered in this way, whose authenticity cannot be verified in any way, in any way whatsoever except if we are to believe the Prosecution investigator, the Defence will then -- will have no choice but to call another 40 witnesses, maybe, to question the authenticity. We are now in a situation that we now seem to be carrying the burden of proof. The ball has been placed in our court, so now they are telling us if you have any problem with any of those, you find the proofs. Everybody knows that all the documents of the Croatian government have been sealed for the next 30 years. But now we are in a position that we bear the burden of proof here, rather than them. Mr. President, the submissions that you just heard about disclosure are also not true. If I rise to my feet, I am going to tell the truth. I know what I have. I know what we received and when we received it. We were to only discuss the two last binders. And as far as the Presidential transcripts are concerned, we submitted a voluminous motion. And let me just add this, not to take any more time, there is a ruling that you made, which is binding to all of us, that document - the documents have to be tendered through witnesses. These witnesses have to be subject to cross-examination. The same documents which we received at the end of the trial, we could have used, we could have used in our cross-examination of other witnesses had we received them in a timely fashion. And having gone through these documents, we saw a number of documents that are not relevant and now we begin to fear one thing; in addition to being saddled with this burden of proof, this may be opening the door for some other things that may have nothing to do with our case, for instance. And now I cannot tell specifically, but there are documents about forced labour of certain detainees. Several hundreds of pages of such documents. My client's name is not mentioned once. So what do these documents serve? We fear that this case may be used to open up the door for some other proceedings, and we think that that is unacceptable. We have completely -- we have complied with your rulings. We were to discuss the last two binders. I suggest that we only limit ourselves to that, to those two binders, and I believe that this really presents the views and positions of our defence, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges concerning these documents? Judge Clark, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, my comments are addressed really to both sides. I've listened very carefully to your arguments, and I find that the arguments are very unpersuasive to the Bench. The Defence are very unspecific in their complaints, and I would have thought that, in the last few days, when you had an opportunity to look at the documents, you might have been able to assist us by saying, "We may have put certain questions to certain witnesses arising out of certain documents in a very specific way and therefore we are prejudiced because we have been deprived of this opportunity." On the other hand, I would have expected that the Prosecution, following the remarks that we made last Thursday, would have explained to us a little more specifically why these documents were not included in the very voluminous binders of documents which we received already or why they weren't referred to by Mr. Prelec when he had prepared a binder of selected documents. I would have liked a little assistance on both sides. You're both repeating the position that you argued last Thursday. We don't seem to have advanced at all, and I'm a little disappointed that you're not making our job a little easier, especially from the Prosecution point of view, because we invited you last week to indicate where you might possibly be prejudiced by the late arrival of these documents. So could you tell us what documents you feel have put you in a worse position than you were had the documents not been tendered at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Judge Clark, it will be my pleasure to answer. During these past three days -- these past several days, all three of us went through all the documents, but I cannot enter a polemic with myself with regard to these documents. I had to have for a polemic a person here who I would debate this document with. We find all of these documents unacceptable. That's why we did not analyse these documents document by document, because I cannot enter a polemic with a document. I can see where the document is like, where it came from, what it speaks of. It's the only thing I can do because I know nothing else about this document. That is why we have restricted ourselves in this way. We were instructed by you to present our views today rather than in writing, and therefore we decided to present our general position for all these documents, not document by document individually, because what I lack is another party to discuss it with. We find all these documents unacceptable, especially from the point of view that was expounded by the Prosecutor. Your Honour, I stand ready to answer any other clarifications you may need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, what I specifically wanted to know was I know that you object to the documents. You're not very happy with them at all, and you've argued very cogently about your feelings about the Zagreb Archive. Whereas you accept the position that the documents came from an archive - Mr. Prelec was very helpful that way - what you mean is that that doesn't mean that the content of the document is true, and that's something that obviously we have to deal with. But have you any additional objections to the tendering of these documents over and above your general argument in relation to the Zagreb Archive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I have a few words on this point? As I understand, those documents could be divided into two categories: One just the lists for the detainees who were taken out for the forced labour; the other documents are some orders or directives with your client's name mentioned specifically on those documents. What's your view towards those two categories of documents? I understand that you mentioned that you might use those lists for the detainees in your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely. Thank you very much for your assistance. The Defence has been thinking along the same lines. That is how we looked at these documents as well, documents that were general, documents that specifically pertained to our client. Of course, in our particular case, you do realise that during these past seven days, we did not have the time to check anything out. We said that we would object to the contents, to the authenticity, rather. We don't know whether this is an authentic document or not, whether it was truly written by the HVO or whoever, or whether it was just invented or whether it has been planted through special warfare. That is something that the Defence would have to check out. And then if they were to be admitted, you can imagine what an extra amount of work we would have to put into all of this. I'm just trying to say that if they had been introduced properly and according to your instructions, had we gone through each and every document with a witness, then that would have been different. If a witness could have been -- could have been in a position to say, "I found this at the Zagreb Archives," and that they knew that before that the documents were in the possession of an intelligence service, we could only enter this kind of a polemic with such a witness. We do not believe the authenticity of these documents. Your Honours, we also have an investigation team of our own. We are going to have other documents, perhaps from Zagreb Archives. And if we prove that they are authentic, if we prove that a person who signed this document had actually compiled the document and signed it, then, of course, we would need lists of detainees and things like that, but in this particular way, the Defence cannot accept this. So even when we find a document, including this one, you really have to go into -- look into matters on the ground. You have to see who wrote this, who signed it, et cetera. That is why we are opposing this. As for the documents that we will be using as the Defence, Your Honour, I assure you today that we are not going to present a single document during our case if we do not have in this courtroom a witness who can testify to the validity of these documents, either the author himself or somebody else who can validly prove the authenticity of these documents. We believe that this is the only course in which truth and justice can be pursued. We have never resorted to tricks of any kind nor do we think that this can be done in a court of law. I think you will agree with me, Judge Clark, that in any legal system, it is only the author who can authenticate a document, either accept this or deny it altogether. So that is the core of the matter. Whoever this may be, we have been denied the opportunity of discussing this with a witness. I simply have to say one more thing to you. My learned friend Mr. Scott, with whom we've had a wonderful cooperation and we are indeed thankful to the Office of the Prosecutor for having helped the Defence so often, I have had very little experience with American laws, but to say that documents are authentic without bringing a single person, one single person to say that this is an authentic document, not even that? And now what can the Defence do? Heaven forbid that you accept these documents, because I will have to bring at least 20 people here to refute them, because we do not have a shred of evidence pointing to the authenticity of these documents. Now, I don't know -- I'm not going to talk about Mr. Prelec now because I don't know whether certain parts that I would like to refer to were protected or not, but thank you. I don't want to keep you any longer on this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. You have to be very concise, if there's nothing new to add to the argument put forward by Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Of course the question is not whether I have anything new to add, but I have been inspired by what Judge Clark said. The situation is considerably different than it was on the 24th of this month when you all told us, Your Honours, that today we will find out what the deadline would be for us to file motions in writing against these documents. On the 25th, after our meeting with Mr. Fourmy, we were informed by you, Your Honours, that today we would present our views verbally, orally at this Status Conference. So that period that we would have from today would be these four days longer because we would get at least seven days, starting today, I hope. So the difference is considerable. We are talking about the time period from Friday until today and then from today onwards, Your Honours. In order to assist the Court by spelling out the objection in more specific terms, I can say laconically that the Defence of Vinko Martinovic does not accept Document P565.3, 579.1, 599.1, 611.2, 612.1, 664.1, 705.1 -- the transcript says 705.1, yes. Then 745.2 and 896. I'm saying this laconically because if I were to object only in this way, Your Honours, this would not be a valid objection. Again, it would just be a partial way of dealing with matters because I would only be dealing with the matters that have to do with my client. It would seem that I am not objecting to the other documents because I'm only narrowly speaking of the interests of my client, and this is the wrong way to do things. Time is brief, and we have been subjected to time pressures from the 3rd of July last year onwards. I do apologise for changing the subject. But the Prosecutor, our learned friend, said that we have been asking for something all the time as if we were trying to obstruct the proceedings. We are not trying to obstruct the proceedings at all. We just want to have a fair trial. So if I were to spell things out this specifically, I think I would be narrowing down the subject altogether, and I don't think that I would be dealing with the problem as a whole but only partially. So we have this objection in principle, in terms of the shortage of time, as we have been stating all along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, are you going to answer the questions asked by Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I'm not sure of the particular questions the Judge may ask. I'm happy to do so. And I also have two very, very brief responses that I must make to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The fundamental point, one of the false arguments that is being made, Mr. President - and I hope the Chamber understands this and I will try not to belabour it - the argument, for instance, that the Defence has been prejudiced in their cross-examination of witnesses stands on a false premise. They were never entitled to receive the documents at any time, so they could not have been prejudiced in not having them for cross-examination. They were not entitled to have them at all until they were tendered at a particular time in Court. So it's simply a false premise to stand up, "We have been prejudiced by not having these documents for cross-examination" when they were never entitled to have them in the first place. That is a decision, once again, that was presumably an informed tactical decision that they made a long time ago. And this goes back in the record for over a year, when Judge Wald was the Pre-Trial judge and she questioned them, "Don't you want document discovery?" "Do you understand under Rule 66(B)?" And this question was repeatedly put to counsel during the pre-trial parts of this case. And their continuing answer was, "No, we don't want them. We don't want the disclosure." So they cannot complain about this disclosure now. In terms of the way the documents were presented, Mr. President, the only thing I can say, with all respect, is the Chamber in the last four months or four and a half months have never given the Prosecution any guidance or any indication that the way it was presenting the documents was deficient. If the Chamber had those concerns, we certainly would have liked to have been given some guidance from the Chamber before we rested our case. We always called the witnesses such as Mr. Prelec, such as Mr. Aguirre, such as Mr. Van Hecke to provide the Chamber with as much information as possible as to how the Office of the Prosecutor obtained those documents. The Chamber never asked us -- with the exception of ten specific exhibits, the Chamber never asked us for more information. And again, we have presented all these exhibits consistent with the Tribunal practice to date, this Tribunal's practice over the past six or seven, eight years. And if the practice is now going to change and the rules are going to change after the Prosecution has rested its case, it will be fundamentally unfair, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, there should be an end to this argument. I give you one minute. One minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One sentence. Thank you. Does this mean that the learned Prosecutor will not object to a single document that the Defence will bring from the Zagreb Archives and will we not have to prove the authenticity of such documents brought from there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I don't think that question is proper at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we have not understood each other very precisely. If the Prosecutor's final argument is that this is from the Zagreb Archives and that there should be no further authentication, then the question is right because that means that then when we bring documents from the Zagreb Archives, they will not be questioned in terms of their authenticity. So I think my question is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, we are not going to pursue this very issue. After consultations with my colleagues, and taking into consideration of the arguments put forward by both sides, this Trial Chamber will reserve its right to make decisions concerning the admission of those two binders of documents at a later stage. So we close the first item of the agenda. The second one is the closing of the Prosecution's case. We just want to know if there is any new information that the Prosecution would like to inform us concerning the closing of the Prosecution's case. We understand that this issue has been brought up during our last sitting already. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the position of the Prosecution has not changed. As I indicated last week, we have called our last witness and closed our case, subject to the outstanding exhibit matters and to the questions -- any questions concerning the so-called wooden rifle. And that is our position and hasn't changed, Mr. President. We do not rest our case unconditionally. We rest our case only on those two reservations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. This Trial Chamber believes that the closing of the Prosecution's case shall be determined according to the admission of the documents, and the Trial Chamber will address the closing of the case in their final written decisions concerning the admission of the documents. It is so decided. The next issue is the Rule 98 bis proceedings. We have been told that the Defence counsel has some intentions to file a motion, which is the motion for acquittal, in accordance with the Rule 98 bis proceedings. Could I hear the Defence counsel on this very issue. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The Defence does intend to file a motion for acquittal. It will be very concise; it will deal only with very specific points. And we will try in a brief, concise, legal manner to explain our objections and also our request for acquittal in accordance with the Rule 98 bis proceedings. That would be all. I hope that this was a concise answer. I know exactly what Rule 98 bis deals with. We believe that the Prosecutor has not produced a shred of evidence to support the indictment; and therefore, according to the various counts in the indictment, we believe that the Prosecution have not proven their case at all, and we intend to prove this in a very concise legal manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to inform you, Mr. President, and also the members of the Chamber, that the Defence of Vinko Martinovic will also act in accordance with Rule 98 bis and move for acquittal. We will follow the indictment paragraph by paragraph, line by line, and it will really be spelled out, therefore, in very concrete terms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, my comment would be more in the nature of an observation, and perhaps a suggestion, respectfully. And it's not in any sense to be presumptuous, and I hope the Chamber will not take it that way, or counsel. But Mr. Meek and I and Mr. Stringer will be able to relate to procedure in our practice, in federal practice in the United States. And I hasten to add we all know this is not U.S. Federal practice; and yet, we all inevitably sometimes draw on our past experience. Your Honour, even in the most complex criminal cases in the United States, and I immodestly would say I have been in some very complex cases, with as many documents or more as in this case, at the close of the Prosecution case, there are normally oral motions for judgement of acquittal. There are normally made -- the Defence attorney stands up on their feet, gives a 20-minute, 25-minute argument. The Prosecution then makes an oral response. And about 49 times out of 50, the Judge rules on the spot. And most times, frankly, the motions are denied because the standard -- it's a high standard, from the Defence perspective, with deference to the case put forward by the Prosecution. I just simply suggest, Mr. President, Your Honours, that it may assist -- I think it would ultimately assist everyone -- if the arguments that counsel puts forward -- and, of course, they are entitled to put forward any good faith argument, and certainly it's not for the Prosecution to stand in the way of Defence rights, but I think it would ultimately be better for everyone if the arguments could be focused on specific items and responses could also be very targeted. Now, when Mr. Krsnik first stood up, I was for a moment encouraged because I thought I heard him say initially "our responses will be very specific," and if I can use the word - I got the impression - somewhat surgical. However, then the discussions of both counsel evolved into such language as "we're challenging the entire indictment paragraph by paragraph, fact by fact, the Prosecution hasn't proved anything." And Mr. President, I would just submit that it would be a poor use of everyone's time to basically have to write final briefs now, when the case is halfway over, what essentially may be what we're talking. Again, it's mostly an observation or suggestion. Everyone in the proceedings would be better served if there are good-faith arguments on particular counts or a particular element of a particular charge, if the motions could be directed in that way. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as an American counsel, as Mr. Scott has certainly just indicated that he is, I am, Mr. Stringer is, and what we do in the United States is certainly not what we do here, I will agree with that, but I don't believe that we will be filing any type of motion for judgement of acquittal which will be tantamount to a final argument. I would also like to say that, as American counsel, I understand Mr. Scott, and we have in America a thing called an open-file policy. And in that open-file policy, once the documents start coming in, then the file is open. To say that Mr. Scott earlier said we didn't have to give him anything so they are not prejudiced is not true. They gave us everything they had, and then this last week they dumped two binders, disgorged two binders upon us at the very end. And now they say since you didn't have a 66(B) motion, we didn't have to. As American lawyers, we know that, we don't expect to file any long -- we are going to concentrate on the issues we believe are weak in the Prosecutor's case. So if it will alleviate Mr. Scott's fear of filing final briefs, I hope he feels better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First of all, I have to remind both parties, this is an International Tribunal - it's not a court in certain countries - so that we have to act in accordance with the Rules of the procedure of this Tribunal, mainly the Rule 98 bis. Secondly, I would like to say that, as we orally ruled last week, this Trial Chamber expects all filings to be precise and directed to the specific charges and the counts. The Defence shall consider that burden lays upon the parties moving for acquittal to provide the Chamber with a clear basis for their motions. The Defence shall therefore provide the Chamber with detailed and specific reasonings. General claims of insufficiency of evidence are not considered to be sufficient by this Trial Chamber. In accordance with Rule 98 bis, the Defence motion is to be filed seven days after the decision of the Trial Chamber has been rendered. That notifies the parties that all the Prosecution evidence has been decided upon and that the Prosecution's case is closed. At the same time, we also would like to remind the Prosecution that response time is reduced pursuant to Rule 127 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to seven days - one week - if so decided on this issue. The next item on our agenda is the status and the preparation of the Defence case. We understand after the closure of the Prosecution's case, we'll soon start the Defence case. So the first question we would like to ask the Defence counsel is: What is the status of the Defence case? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you know, between July of last year and now, the Defence could only focus and deal with the ongoing proceedings day and night. So we have to say that we did not have much time during this phase of the trial to really address the issue of witnesses, but we are turning to that as of today. I am waiting for point four of today's agenda to present all the arguments regarding the relative number of witnesses, depositions, et cetera. I think that we should clarify all those matters in point four. Oh, I'm sorry. My colleagues are just telling me that that is exactly what we are now discussing. I apologise. My misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Krsnik. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is really the point that we have been waiting for for quite some time. We believe that it is crucial for the -- in the continuation of trial, and it is crucial to get enough time for preparation, and I'm going to try to really keep it -- to surgically address all these issues; in other words, cut as close to the bone as I can. We have been receiving documents since July of 2001, and the initial witness list was 350. We started dealing with those, and we did not know until the depositions were first taken which of these witnesses would be called. Of course, this is the Prosecutor's right, his tactics. We could not obviously check each and every witness in detail. But before the depositions, we received a list of 30 witnesses. It was whittled away to 16, and then we dealt with those. About a week before the beginning of trial, we received a list of 66 witnesses and eventually, I think, that 53 or 4 were called. In other words, the list was always subject to change. We learned of this two or three days before the start of the trial. In the period between the depositions and the beginning of the trial itself, as serious lawyers before this serious Tribunal -- Tribunal, we spent one month waiting to see who it was that was going to be called, and this is why we rose to our feet and said we were not prepared. However, we still did the best we could, always wondering whether we did the best or we could have done better. And our general position, which I think is the one that should be shared in this institution, was that the factor of time cannot be the prevalent principle when fairness of the trial is concerned. This is the position that our client has, and I think that it's something which should be shared by everyone. The interest of justice should be paramount. And in order to arrive at justice, we, Your Honours, need time. Please don't misunderstand me. I will be very specific and tell you what time we need for which part of the trial. We cannot serve justice unless we're well prepared. I will not be able to face the son of my client if, let's say, ten years from now - and now I'm taking certain liberty - if there was a document which could have helped his father and I was unable to find it because I didn't have the time. There are 10.000 binders in the Zagreb Archive. We don't know the exact number of the documents. Perhaps the Prosecution knows because they have ten investigators there every day. The Defence is limited even financially, so we can only hire two people, and they have so far reviewed about 30 per cent, which means 3.000 binders. So we have 7.000 to go. Next there is a sizeable archive in Sarajevo, the ABiH archives, the government, the Presidency of BiH. So far, we have written I don't know how many letters asking for permission to gain access to these documents. So far, we have not received anything, but this access has been allowed to all the lawyers who represent the Muslim defendants. Edina Residovic, Halid Balijagic, and every -- Vasvija Vidovic, and everybody who is representing Bosniak accused were given access to these archives, but not the counsel of Mladen Naletilic. I'm going in the field soon, and if we're unsuccessful, I'm going to turn to you and ask for assistance. However, I believe that reason will prevail and that the Defence of Mladen Naletilic will be given access to these archives. Once we are given access, what are we to expect? How many binders, how many documents, and how much time do we need? It is the investigators' job, but I at least need to have enough information. At the same time, I have to deal with the witnesses that we need to present. The third and most important point, Your Honours, is that -- and again I don't know whether in the American jurisdiction or in the practice of this Tribunal it is the case that they don't need to be objective but only look for inculpatory material. And we heard in this -- during -- in this courtroom that this is the kind of documents that they were still looking for and the kind of witnesses that they were looking for, which means that I have to go to Madrid, for instance, to go to the SpaBat archives. This is hypothetical, of course, but I need to see and find out what documents are there. We had two witnesses here. Perhaps I need to call some other witnesses. I don't know what to expect there, but I would not be following my conscience if I didn't do so. How about ECMM? Each of the ECMM countries who send monitors have their own archives. Is there a central database? We heard two gentlemen from the ECMM who gave whatever evidence they gave, but what about all the other documents signed by Jose -- Jesus and I don't know who else. Mr. Thebault. Where is the central archive? I could not in good conscience do it without really taking time to 17 blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. check all these documents. It's a very large trial. It's a -- we have neglected our families. We have neglected our professional pursuits in our home jurisdictions to focus exclusively on this here. And of course, you understand that all this is being done in the interests of justice. And we will have a much tougher job. The ball has been placed in our court, and our burden has been increased considerably. We will have to present the -- the proof of innocence here. But in order to facilitate matters, in order to be more effective, we have done -- we have conducted comprehensive interviews, and we have had discussions with both the -- our learned friends from the Prosecution and with Mr. Fourmy. We have presented our positions as best we could there. I do not want to belabour this, but I want to be as specific as I can, of course. And I apologise to the interpreters for being fast. The Defence is minded to breaking up their presentation of evidence into two parts, just as the Prosecution did. The one that we believe is the most effective and the fastest was to have depositions taken in Mostar, in the building of the overhauled and renovated building of the higher court, which is fully equipped for taking of these depositions, and our clients -- I should limit myself to my client, but my client will waive his right to be present there. So we need a very small team of people, interpreters and the technical staff. And we propose this because we have 30 witnesses whose examination-in-chief would last between 30 minutes and one hour apiece. So we can conclude that we could deal with two witnesses a day just in a single morning, let's say, if we work 9.00 to 2.00. As these witnesses live and work there, we would have very little need of the Victim and Witness Unit because they can just go home when they're done. The third and most important point is that we all would like to see this Trial Chamber or this Tribunal appear at the scene where all this happened. Perhaps we could even go to Sovici and Doljani. Of course this would depend on your ruling, but in my discussions with Mr. Fourmy, this was also floated as an idea. I believe that you may be aware of it. So I think that we would deal with about a half of our witnesses, so to speak, in a very expedient manner. The witnesses who I believe would appear in this courtroom would be the ones that I believe Your Honours should hear. There would be about 30. I don't have a final list. That would also depend on some of your rulings. But of course we will comply with all the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in providing them. In this group of witnesses, we would have witnesses who would deal with the Background and General Allegations, and we believe that some of these witnesses are crucial witnesses for these matters, and they would also include expert witnesses. It is our estimate that we could comply with all the deadlines and the defence of the first accused, Mr. Naletilic. We believe that our case could be concluded around July 15th. Of course, my learned friend will present his part of case, but I believe that we can comply with all the -- with the time line schedule provided by the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, I have been as specific as I can. I wanted to give you an idea of how large this work is that is ahead of us. We believe that, in the light of that, we should start on the 15th of April. After the depositions, we could start on the 15th of May, and I think we could be done by the 15th of July. And again, don't hold me to the day, but we believe that, with all things considered, the whole case could be finished by the middle of September or end of September. And I don't know -- in the interests of justice -- and I may have been using this word a little bit too frequently. I think that in the interest of justice, this time line is adequate. We are not asking for anything that would be outside of the scope of the Statute. We need to have sufficient amount of time, as the Statute provides, and we really have done our best to bring it within the time frame that I presented. And if Your Honours agree with it, it would still place the Defence counsel in the position to really work day and night to comply with it. So we would not waste any time. My colleague is telling me that the 15th of April is when we would start with depositions, not with the trial itself. Your Honour, we believe that if the Defence would have sufficient time to prepare its witnesses, the witnesses would give their evidence in a speedier way. We would not waste any undue time. I would not have to wrestle with witnesses, so to speak, to arrive at what I need and to deal with. I think that it would be much more effective and much speedier for this case. Your Honour, I need to point out another fact: Some documents that are being forwarded to us from our investigators who are working in the archives, some of these have been submitted but for translation, and we have only received about 10 percent. We don't know what is going to happen with those. We fear that these documents may not be ready at the time of trial because the translation unit needs time to have them translated. We have a suggestion. I am almost certain that the translations are not going to be ready by this time. Perhaps some documents, some shorter ones perhaps, may be interpreted in the courtroom by courtroom interpreters, because we have experience from other trials, and I have a personal experience. Some documents which I have submitted for translation back in September, they deal with some of the -- of our expert witnesses, and they are still not ready. And the documents that we have submitted for our own case are still all pending at this point. I don't want to take any more time, Your Honours. This is as succinct as I could present our positions. And with all due respect to this Chamber, to our profession, and my conscience, I really don't know what my own reaction is going to be, or my client's, if we find out that we are squeezed for time and that we will not be able to prepare adequately. I don't know if I can allow myself, with all my experience as an attorney, to deal with this case which already is a part of history. And it is definitely going to be part of the history of this segment of time if I believe that I cannot allow myself not to be well-prepared for it. We are not to blame for being brought in a situation, and this includes you, that we have been served with an indictment which -- where there are allegations that no witness, no document can really deal with properly. This is -- nothing happened by accident. Nothing just fell out of the sky. Of course, we cannot start with the 15th Century to understand this. But we are forced, given how the indictment has been framed, to present expert witnesses because those of us who lived in this area during these unfortunate years and this terrible war, and our families both in Bosnia and in Croatia may have certain information, but you have it -- a much harder job because you come from different jurisdictions, and you did not live through these experiences. So it may be harder for you to understand everything that happened. And so we are here to try to help you, because we would like to help you to reach as just a decision as is possible. This doesn't concern me. This is the -- it concerns the fate of my client. In order for me to fight for justice, I need time. The indictment, such as it is, requires certain amount of preparation. We need to respond. We need to answer the allegations. This is why, Your Honours, I believe that one month, in the name of justice, is meaningless. And if I may add something else, Your Honours, the pressure has been great. Nobody -- we talked to other lawyers from other trials, and nobody is subject to such pressure as we have been. We have observed all the deadlines. You have been patient with us. Sometimes we may have been off the mark. We are very grateful for all your suggestions and all your assistance. But the Defence still is not clear as to why such time pressure on this trial. In some other cases, they already have had one month worth of breaks, and we have started practically in parallel. I'm not going to take any more of your time, Your Honours. I, myself, on behalf of my client ask, insist; please, give us enough time so we can prepare adequately. You do not want me not to do my job properly. You do not want me to look as if I don't know my job. I think that we have been correct. I think that we have done all we could to help you reach, to arrive at the truth. And I say the truth such as it is. This Defence will not call any witnesses tu quoque. We are too experienced for that. We are not going to point fingers elsewhere in order to justify certain crimes. Of course, we know that one crime does not justify another crime. We need to focus on whether and what our client did. But as far as the General Allegations are concerned, we will -- we are the least satisfied in the way that part of the indictment has been presented; and without adequate preparation, we are not going to be able to fully illuminate that part. Again, let me tell you, we are going to comply with all the deadlines and all the schedules. And I would want to assure this Trial Chamber that we will be its right hand in our efforts to comply with all the deadlines that you set out for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krsnik, for your submissions. Frankly speaking, I share some of the views you expressed. For instance, we also believe that the interests of justice should be paramount, which requires a balance between the fairness and expedition of our trials. But there are still some questions that we would like to ask you. Maybe we'll reserve it after the break. For instance, up to now, we still don't know how many witnesses are you going to call altogether and how many documents are you going to tender in your case. And as for how to conduct your case, you mentioned clearly that you have not invoked the principle of tu quoque, which should be appreciated by this Trial Chamber, but we could not agree with you that you have to prove the innocence of your client. We believe that your client should be presumed innocent until proved guilty, so there's no need for you to prove the innocence of your client. What you have to do is just to attack the evidence presented by the Prosecutor during their case. If we have some doubts, some doubts beyond a reasonable doubt on those evidence, that would be a successful defence for your client. The second issue: I would like to say that this is an International Tribunal rather than a truce and conciliation committee. We are not interested in political matters. What we are going to address is the individual criminal responsibilities which might involve the fate of your client in this very case. This is the initial response from me. I guess my colleagues may have some other questions to ask you after the break. So shall we break now, and we'll resume at 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Are you ready to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First and foremost, perhaps an additional bit of explanation in addition to what I have already said today while trying to explain the motion related to Defence preparations. Everything that I said to you today is based on the talks, the exhaustive talks I had with the distinguished Mr. Fourmy. The time I asked for are our absolutely minimal requirements. The Defence is afraid that it simply cannot go below that. Again, I repeat on the basis of what we discussed with Mr. Fourmy. With regard to all other matters, we abide by what we said in the paper. As for witnesses, Your Honour, the Defence would be the happiest of all if they could give the exact number today. We can only give an approximation because we lack some information in this regard. We also need to have some decisions taken by this Trial Chamber and also developments that would be based on that. We can say today in principle, proceeding from the position that we hope that you will take, that the total number of witnesses could be around 60. You will realise that this number is due to the fact that the burden of proof lies with the Defence of Mr. Naletilic with regard to the General Allegations, but we hope our colleagues will help you with this. When we finally hear what your ruling will be, we will be able to tell you what the exact number would be. Because of some of the decisions based on documents will be accepted, you understand that we will have to bring in new witnesses. Also, this number depends on one of the last witnesses. I can't remember his pseudonym now. We were not informed about this witness until we got this person's statement from our learned friend. This was an altogether new development, and we will have to deal with this person separately. But I don't think that the number involved will be more or less than ten if your decisions will be the way the Defence believes they will be; or conversely, the number could go up. And yet if things are altogether different, perhaps it could go down. I shall tell you quite frankly, as I always have been doing to this Trial Chamber, especially because the Defence was never engaged in any kind of tactics or will we ever do that, right now we are in the possession of 20.000 documents that we collected over the past few years. Most of them are from the Zagreb Archives, a vast majority of these documents. As for others, we will have to make do because the Defence simply does not have the kind of possibilities that the Office of the Prosecutor has. And I hope the Prosecutor, my learned friend, will not mind that I am saying this. Of course, we are not going to produce all of these documents here. We will have to group them, and we will have to make a selection as to what we are going to present here. We are still compiling documents, though, because according to our assessment, in 10.000 binders, there could be about 100.000 documents. This is a very general statement. Now we have to look at the Sarajevo archives, so to speak, and also SpaBat, perhaps BritBat, SpaBat. However, I assure you that we are only going to present high-quality documents in this courtroom, and we will try to keep the number reasonable. We hope that we will not be producing more than 1.000 documents in this courtroom. If there are any other questions, I'm prepared to answer them. I don't know if you are satisfied with the answer I have already provided. If you have any additional questions, I'm here to answer them. But this is more or less what we have to say today. But again, as I said, all of this is a statement of principle, because it all depends ultimately on the decisions that you will make, and a great deal hinges on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krsnik. Could I hear from Mr. Seric on this very point. Mr. Seric, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I am not going to argue now. I'm going to leave that for my closing argument. First, the situation as far as the Defence of my client is concerned: It, of course, is closely linked to what the indictment says. What am I trying to say? The indictment gives the first accused supremacy over the second accused person. It is precisely for that reason that our two Defence teams decided to present the Defence in the same way. That is to say that we have the common allegations in the indictment and the counts in the indictment, and we will try to address these individually and together. Then there are individual counts that will be addressed by the two Defences individually. So the situation is on the basis of this supremacy from the indictment, the Defence of the first accused has taken upon itself a certain obligation, and we are going to help them in this process to deal with background witnesses. That is to say, the Defence of the first accused will deal with these witnesses. We have put ourselves in a waiting position, so to speak. As for the time we need to prepare our Defence is the same time because we cannot and should not act separately from each other. So first, the Defence of the first accused would present their case, as Mr. Krsnik said. It is not only that we accept this; we wholeheartedly support it with the time frames proposed by Mr. Krsnik. He is asking this Trial Chamber, and we support this. And we also kindly ask the Trial Chamber to start on the 15th of April. After the Defence of the first accused is completed, then we would start our Defence. And I cannot tell you exactly when that would be. Your Honours, we have already completed part of the Defence preparations; however, that is insufficient at this point in time. We heard that what remains to be dealt with is a lion's share of the overall work we have to complete. As the Prosecution case is winding up, we see that we have to do a great deal of investigation in the field, and we will have to look for the traces and microtraces, so to speak, at sites related to count 5. The Prosecution says that this is the body of Nenad Harmandic. After that, if we manage to get from the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the east part of Mostar all these traces and microtraces, we will have to undergo expertise. We will have to go through a forensic court expert and also through another court expert. And we hope, with your assistance, Your Honours, that our request put forth to the Ministry of the Interior in Mostar will be met. With your help, I'm saying, because nobody has ever accommodated us there. I don't want to enter any kind of polemic with the OTP, but at one point our colleague speaks of reciprocal disclosure. I repeat today, Your Honours, we had nothing to offer to the Prosecutor by way of evidence. Nobody wanted to accommodate us. We were not in a position to get any evidence whatsoever. Your Honours, we will have to obtain the medical documents that are related to new developments in these proceedings. We did not know about that earlier. We found out only during the proceedings themselves, and we will have to call a psychiatrist as an expert witness because one of the crown witnesses was the one that I just referred to. So we will have to deal with this matter as well. Also, we had to deal with a witness who spoke of a unit that coincided, not in terms of location but in terms of time. It overlapped -- this is the Penavic unit. And this is a new development for us altogether. And we will have to find out exactly what took place within this unit so that we could present this to the Trial Chamber in order to be in a position to distinguish between these things that seem to overlap. That is to say, what our client has done and what was perhaps done by someone else. There is yet another question that has been opened, the so-called issue of wooden rifles. Why am I saying that this is still an open question? The Prosecutor has left open the possibility for these wooden rifles to appear in this courtroom, and then we will have to undergo expertise in this respect to see whether they were forged and whether they were perhaps made after the war. Now, what else do we need in terms of establishing the time that is necessary? Presidential transcripts. I hope you don't misunderstand what I'm saying. We have to -- if you admit this, we will have to contact every one of the persons who took part in these discussions. We will have to ask all these people to testify here, bring them here, because we think this is the only right way to proceed to see whether these are authentic, whether they took part in these discussions at all, whether their words were recorded faithfully, or whether all this is just a pile of -- I'm not going to say what. We heard during the cross-examination of one witness that he knew nothing special about this, so then we will be -- we will have to deal with these 10 or 15 witnesses whose names appear in the Presidential transcript. Your Honours, we will perhaps present a proposal, as Mr. Krsnik has already done. Perhaps you come to Mostar to see how long the Bulevar was, how wide it was, and these 70 metres that were allegedly held by my client. You should see what percentage this actually is. Your Honours, good and thorough preparations do not waste time but, rather, help us save time, and I think that this will be the case in the presentation of our evidence as well. Finally, may I say that no matter how contradictory this may sound, it is very difficult for the principles of fairness and of economy with time be kept in proportion. However, I hope that you will take both into account in terms of the time that this Defence needs for preparing their work properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, the first thing I would like to say is that this Trial Chamber will do its utmost to help you to prepare your case. If you need any assistance from this Trial Chamber, you just make that request. We will do whatever we can in this respect. The second thing I want to stress is that to have the trial conducted fairly and expeditiously is also the right of your client. They have been in the Detention Unit for quite a long time, more than two years. They are entitled to have a fair and expeditious trial. And thirdly, Mr. Seric, you still did not answer the questions that I put to Mr. Krsnik, that is: How many witnesses are you going to call, approximately, and is there any evidence you are going to tender through your witnesses? That's what we want to know at this stage. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed I omitted to mention this last thing. In our written submissions, the Defence said that it had 80 witnesses. However, during our talks and after our talks with our colleague Mr. Fourmy, we came to the conclusion that the minimal number that this Defence needs in order to present its own case to this Trial Chamber, and everything that is important in order to prove the innocence that we have been asserting from day one, the total number, in a word, would be about 50 witnesses. So when I said that the Defence has at -- this joint view, if Mr. Krsnik would have 60 witnesses and we'd have, say, 60 witnesses, it would be about 120 witnesses. However, this is a question of pure mathematics. Now, what else did I miss? Oh, yes, documents. Documents. As I said at the very outset, all the documents that this Defence has are the documents that our learned friends of the Prosecution gave to us. We do not have a single new document. If we do have any new documents, if we get any new documents, or if we have some expert opinions, we are going to introduce them through our experts and through our witnesses. May God help us in this and may we have the most complete documentation possible to support our assertions. But as I've said, until now, we have nothing else to introduce except for these expert opinions. And now the documents of the Prosecutor that were disclosed to us until now and that were not introduced, that were not admitted into evidence and that the Defence will want to tender are documents that are already in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we hear the response from the Prosecution? Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. First off, a few responses, specific responses, and then I'll return to specifically the Prosecution positions on some of the issues raised as we have discussed them among ourselves in the last several days. First, Mr. President, we are not sure at all where counsel obtain the number of 300, that there was ever a witness list comprising anything like 300 Prosecution witnesses. On the -- in October 2000, long before the trial started, we had submitted a list of 113 witnesses. At the end of the day, so to speak, we in fact called or offered the testimony of 83 witnesses, 57 live - that is, in Court - 16 by deposition, 10 by transcript from other cases. So you will see that given the nature of this work, 83 out of 113 was -- is not too far off the mark and that our list was not over-broad or overinclusive but not too far away from what the final numbers in fact were. So we said more than a year before this trial -- or almost a year before this trial started that there was a witness list, and witness summaries, I might add, of approximately 113 witnesses. I'm also not sure of the basis for counsel's assertion that the OTP has ten investigators at the archive every day. I'm sure that Madam del Ponte would be very interested to know how many employees are at the archive. I have no reason to think it's anything like that, with maybe the exception of one or two very short periods of time over the past two years. Mr. Krsnik said that they have conducted - his exact words on this point were "comprehensive interviews," but I have to point out to the Chamber, to date the Prosecution has not received a single Defence witness statement. They apparently exist. There have been comprehensive interviews, but we have yet to receive a Defence witness statement. Mr. Krsnik, of course, in an effort to be optimistic, mentions that they want to do 30 witnesses by deposition, and tells the Chamber that many of these witnesses would be anywhere from approximately a half hour to one hour. Well, not to be more of a pessimist, Mr. President, but I have to indicate that a good number of the Prosecution witnesses in its case, the direct examinations were often not far from about an hour. So to say that a direct examination of a witness will take something approximately around an hour, and therefore one can extrapolate that it should be quite quick and efficient, I'm afraid does not necessarily lead to that conclusion. These things do take considerable amount of time. But again, I'll come back to some of the specific issues in a few moments. I think, Mr. President, we submit that the comments about the Presidential transcripts is really engaging in a great deal of hyperbole. For the Defence to say, "We're going to be required to call every single person who may have participated in one of those meetings or were present in the meetings," I think is unrealistic and not genuine. But it's apparently intended as, if I can call it, a scare tactic against the Chamber to presumably discourage the Chamber from admitting that very important evidence. I submit that's a gross overstatement of what would be expected. Mr. President, in terms of specifics - in terms of the recess, the Prosecution stated that, with due regard to all the outstanding matters, the work that the Chamber needs to do presumably, and the work - some reasonable time for the Defence to prepare, we have stated our position, which continues to this moment, that the trial should begin again on the Monday, the 4th of March, 2002 with the beginning of the Defence case. That is our position. We think that is in line, if not indeed generous, with most of the practice before the Tribunal to date. Many of the breaks have certainly been much less, much, much less, in longer trials than the time requested by these accused. We would remind the Chamber, of course, that Rule 65 ter (G) requires each Defence to file the following: A list of witnesses; a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify; (c), the points in the indictment as to which the witness will testify, et cetera. Of course, again we have not received any of that information, presumably nor has the Chamber. They are also required to provide a list of exhibits, which, of course, we have not seen. Mr. President, one point we had -- one of our prior filings, and I think this even goes back to a filing we made to the Chamber on the 29th of November last year in connection with the notice that we were requesting, we had at one point done our own analysis of the amount of time or amount of notice given on particular Prosecution witnesses. And at that particular point in the trial, we simply chose the first 20 Prosecution witnesses. We found that on -- that no witness, not a single witness, with the exception of one who was called because -- at the Registry's request out of turn, with the exception of that witness, no witness was called by the Prosecutor on less than 19 days' notice prior to that witness taking the stand. And the average -- that was the shortest time. The average notice given between the time that we said we would be calling this witness and the time that that witness actually testified on the stand was 35 days. We asked the -- the Prosecution asks to be given similar notice. In terms of depositions, Mr. President, our position is that we really cannot respond very much because, as we've stated to the Defence in our meeting last week and also have indicated in our papers, none of the information has been provided for us to make any response. We don't have a list of the proposed deposition witnesses; we don't have a summary of what the deposition witnesses will testify to, nor the justifications for why they are appropriate as deposition witnesses. And the Chamber may recall, when the Prosecution proposed deposition witnesses, it took a considerable number of months and rulings and second series of rulings before all that was sorted out. And we were required to do all those things; give the witnesses by name, summarise them, and give justification as to why, under Rule 71, they were appropriate for deposition treatment. We've received none of that information from the Defence. So we simply cannot respond other than to say the Rules provide for depositions under appropriate circumstances. We don't know what the Defence has in mind. When that information is provided, we will certainly review it and make further responses at that time. In terms of the timing of the depositions, if there are any depositions, Your Honours, it is the considered view of the Prosecution side that we're not sure it would be the most efficient actually to take the depositions at the very beginning because it may very well be that as the Defence cases start, the Chamber might give the Defence some guidance. The Defence case might narrow. Once we have an -- we don't know what the Defence is. We don't know what the Defence is. Once the defence becomes known, it very well may be that these depositions are not needed at all, or may be less or may be under different circumstances. So it strikes us, we respectfully submit, that to take the depositions at the beginning, before knowing any of this information or the shape or direction of the Defence, could be a huge waste of time and resources. So we ask the Chamber to consider not taking depositions until after more about the Defence case is known, and so that both the Prosecution and the Chamber can respond as appropriate and give such reaction and guidance as might be appropriate to the nature of the Defence case. For instance, let me be more specific, only by example. Mr. Krsnik says today that the Defence is not going to put forth a tu quoque Defence. I am happy to hear him say that. I hope he will forgive me if I receive that with some skepticism or at least a "wait and see" attitude. And that's why I say cite an example. What if the 30 deposition witnesses -- only by example: What if the 30 deposition witnesses are all or most of them tu quoque witnesses? Then why should we do those depositions? Why should we spend the time doing that? And that is the problem, Mr. President. We have a vacuum of information. And we don't know whether they are appropriate or not, or if the timing is appropriate because we have no information. The location of the depositions, Mr. President: In principle, as we've stated in our papers, we believe depositions should take place in The Hague. That is the position that the Prosecution was put into at the insistence of the Defence. The reality is that one of the things I think we all learned -- and when I say all of us, including the court staff and both sides or all sides -- the taking of depositions requires virtually the identical staff and resources as a trial, with the exception of Your Honours. It is labour- and time- and resource-intensive; and at the end of the day, it is much easier to do those things here with the facilities at hand than it is to do them outside The Hague.
