Also, frankly, we feel it would give the Defence potentially an advantage and access to local witnesses that might on balance be more willing to come to a deposition in Mostar than they would be to come to The Hague. And as has been said many times in the course of these proceedings, what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. The Prosecution did not have the opportunity to take depositions in the field, we think it's only fair that the same rule applies, with one possible exception we do allow in our papers; we're trying to be reasonable. If there is indeed a specific showing that particular deposition witnesses are, in fact, appropriate and, in fact, very limited in their testimony, proposed testimony, we would entertain further -- I'm just saying we have left the door cracked open. We would entertain further whether some very limited depositions might be suitable or appropriate outside The Hague. But in principle, we think they should be in The Hague. There has also been mention, although not so much today but in the prior papers, there has been reference to videolink, and our response to that is the same. We don't know who, where, or what. Clearly, the Rules do provide for videolink on the appropriate showings by counsel. We just don't know what those showings are. I think, Mr. President, those are our basic positions. We would seek -- we certainly seek to have full disclosure as required by 65 ter. We would like to have, obviously, a Defence witness list for both Defence teams as soon as possible, we'd like to have exhibit lists as soon as possible, and we would like to have the notice of the order of witnesses as soon as possible, again at least commensurate or roughly commensurate with the times provided by the Prosecution. We see no justification for any different rules in this regard. This is not trial by ambush. It is not a violation of the Defence right not to incriminate himself, for instance; that if indeed he chooses to present a case, then he must do so fairly as well; and it isn't a question of hiding the ball. So the Prosecution, Mr. President, I must say feels quite strongly that these notices and the disclosures are only fair and necessary for the Prosecution to proceed in a way that's fair to the Prosecution and fair indeed to the International Community. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And there's one question we would like to address to Defence counsel. That is, according to the Rule 65 ter (G), after the close of the Prosecutor's case and before the commencement of the Defence case, the Defence have to file certain documents, that is, the list of witnesses, the summary of the testimony of those witnesses, as well as the list of exhibits. We would like to hear the views from Defence counsel on this very issue. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was first going to respond to my learned friend and some of his submissions, or shall I first answer your question, the question you just posed to me? Your Honour, the Defence, at this point, is not aware of a number of things, and we will provide summaries of all our witnesses in compliance with your ruling. At this point, we have been speaking with people who are our potential witnesses. We still don't know whether they will agree to come and who among them will come and give evidence. I understand Mr. Scott when he says the Defence should be working properly. He has about 500 staff. I only have two hands, and I cannot be in two places at the same time. Your Honours, I have to say that from July of last year, we did not have a single second, and I don't understand how the Prosecutor thinks that we could have juggled five different things. Regarding the witnesses, now that -- when we arrive at the specific witnesses, when they agree and they say, "Yes, I will come and give evidence," I can only speak in general terms. We were speaking -- we had about 350 potential witnesses by the Prosecution. That was two months before the depositions. It was the first time at that time that we heard who the deposition witnesses would be. And then we received a revised list and that kept revising during the trial itself, and this is what we had. I don't know. Perhaps the spirit of my language is different from the one that is being taken in the transcript, but do you really believe that I would say something, I would dare say something that is not true here in this courtroom? The same thesis is being presented: We've had time and we should be prepared. No, we did not have enough time. The Prosecutor knows fully well that he provided us a witness list two days before the trial. And why is he now resorting to stylistic and different orations to misrepresent the facts? We knew two months before the trial -- we had a list of 30 witnesses, rather than 15, who actually showed up, and this is what we're trying to avoid. We want to be specific and precise in order not to waste any time. Had the Prosecutor lived by his own words, we would not be on our -- we would not have been on our feet when we said that we were not prepared. It is a different situation if you deal with 350 witnesses or 200 witnesses or if we're dealing with 57 witnesses. Or -- I -- if I -- if I am dealing with a hundred documents, why not have all hundred documents right away and then I can deal with them all at the time? If we say half an hour to one hour per witness, this is because we're trying to be effective. And then the Prosecutor gets up and says, "We don't know who the witnesses are going to be and how long they're going to take." Are we considered not serious enough when we say what we say? If I said this, then I will present the witnesses as I said that I would to give me the arguments which would counter the arguments of the Prosecutor. For instance, Your Honours, "Witness X, are you a member of the Convicts Battalion?" And he will say, "No, I never was." And I will say, "Thank you very much. This completes my direct examination." I don't know how long the cross will take. So I think that I was very clear. So I don't know why we are resorting to these figures of speech and all. And I don't know. This is why I invoked the spirit of language. Maybe the spirit does not carry over into the English language. If we said, Your Honours, that the Prosecutor doesn't have the right to say -- it doesn't -- it cannot speak about the time factor, because at the time of the indictment, they should have been ready for trial. Your Honours, the indictment was issued in December 1999. So in January of 2000, they should have been ready for trial, and look what happened. From September -- from September 1999 until October 2001, they continuously interviewed witnesses. In other words, the Prosecutor had additional two years, and now we're asked to do the same job in four weeks? Your Honours, we're all new to this Tribunal. In the Blaskic case, the trial went on for three years. In the Kordic case, it went on for a year and a half. The Kupreskic case, it was one and a half years. Blaskic was a single accused, Kordic two, and Kupreskic five, all with many fewer counts of the indictment. So are the rules different? And the rules were that they had 14 days of hearings and 14 days of breaks. And now we are trying to package the Defence within four weeks. And this is not an American-style trial, and this is not a truth and reconciliation commission, as you brilliantly put it, Your Honour. So we also have to tackle the policy issues because it is in the indictment. And we're supposed to do all this within four weeks and that would be fair? I think that it is in the interest of the Prosecution to have a fair trial just as everybody else has that interest. And I think that if we find that certain counts in the indictment are proved not true, I think that the Prosecutor should also feel happy that the truth was found. So it is in the interest of justice that -- I think that we -- it is something that is shared, and I think that the Prosecution should support us in our quest for it. We should not resort to petty tactics here. Your Honours, I think it is very clear to both you and the -- as it is to the Defence why we had the depositions in The Hague. It is because these were the Prosecution witnesses and our clients wanted to be present to hear their accusors. I think it is very clear, they don't need to be present at depositions of our own witnesses. And it is really because we wanted to do things as efficiently as possible and also for the reasons of judicial economy. And you can check that with the Registry: How much is the cost of travel of 30 witnesses who come here, or those who take their -- of whom depositions are taken locally? When I said 10 to 15 minutes per witness, I said that as a rule of thumb. Based on what the witnesses here have said and the evidence they have given, we may have to go through another 90 witnesses. They may just testify to whether they were members of the Convicts Battalion or not, so it could take no more than 5 minutes to take a solemn declaration and then the facts that they need to say. I think that I was very clear. I don't want to belabour this. And I think that at this point, both the Defence and Prosecution should work in concert on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. I give you three minutes, if you have something new to add, but we are really --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no, I'll be done right away. Just to answer the question, because you directed it to both counsel: We will really observe the 65 ter (G)(i)(a) but we will not provide the full names of witnesses but rather their initials due to the situation in Mostar, which is full of -- which the Trial Chamber is fully aware, and we will use the same attitude that the Prosecution had towards us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after hearing all the submissions from the both parties, there are still matters this Trial Chamber would like to address to the both parties. The Defence counsel said that in some other cases that take longer time, for instance, Blaskic case, three years, another case, one year and a half, I have to say that different cases have different situations that have to be dealt with. And this Tribunal, frankly speaking, has been criticised for the delay of the trials, especially during the pre-trial stage. And I would like to also draw your attention to the breaks between the Prosecution's case and the Defence case. If you look into the jurisprudence before this Tribunal, you could see the longest break is two months. That is the Blaskic case, which is a very big case indeed, and it has not been finished yet. Normally, it is only two or three weeks for the break. The second matter I would like to address is the number of witnesses. Presuming that the Defence counsel is right that the Prosecution has potential witness of 350 at the very beginning, but actually they successfully reduced the number of witnesses to 83, of which 57 we heard in this courtroom, and 16 by deposition, and 10 by transcripts, which is more or less within the limits prescribed by the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Wald. I remember very clearly that the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Wald, requested the Prosecution to reduce the number of witnesses to 50, and the time frame was ten weeks. This Trial Chamber found that we are very surprised to hear that the Defence counsel altogether will have 120 witnesses. We would like to apply the principle of equality of arms and set the prerequisite of the number of the witnesses as the same number as the Prosecution's case. That is, 50 witnesses, and ten weeks' time frame, in principle. Of course, it's also subject to certain variations, but we only hear those number of the witnesses in this courtroom and during that time frame. We also believe that it is the obligation of the Defence counsel to submit their pre-Defence filings in accordance with Rule 65 ter (G), and meetings between the two parties should be encouraged to find agreement of the time frame for disclosure among themselves and call upon this Trial Chamber if there's no agreement possible, or if there's any agreement that is violated. As for the specific timetable, this Trial Chamber will take into consideration of the submissions by the both parties during this Status Conference and make our decisions in the orders at a later stage. We hope the commencement of the Defence case will start as soon as possible. We could not delay without any proper cause. It is so decided. The last item is Item 5. I wonder whether there's any issues that both parties would like to bring to the attention to this Trial Chamber at this stage. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was brought to my attention by your staff there was a question about one of the prior witnesses who had indicated a witness name being mentioned and whether that statement had ever been taken. It was, and in fact I thought it had been provided; but if it wasn't by accident, then we're certainly happy to provide it to both the Chamber and counsel at this time, although, again, I thought we had. But we do have that. This is -- it's a protected witness, so I won't say the name. I assume that's what Madam Registrar is providing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that Mr. Krsnik specifically asked this question during the last sitting. I hope this statement will dispel any doubt about the possible disclosure of the identity of the witnesses. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, just a couple of points: Let me first comment on what was just said, and then I would want to raise an important issue which I think we will only start today. I would like to say this: This case has more counts than the Blaskic case has. If the Blaskic case was very big, then this one is still bigger. If we want fair trials, everything has to be taken into account. I respect what you said when you say that we cannot compare cases in every respect. If somebody has a trial what lasts for three years, let's say a year and a half the Prosecution case, and the Defence had more time to prepare and was given two months -- I really don't want to draw these parallels. And we had five or seven -- I'm not going to compare my case with the case where there were five to seven attorneys at the Defence. I'm awaiting your decision to see when the Prosecution case is officially closed, and I think that the clock will start running from that point on for the Defence. I want to assure you, though, with the deepest respect for everything you have said, Your Honour, I cannot become an adventurist, and anything short of full preparation for this case is adventurism. The consequences may be disastrous, and I will have to deal with my conscience. I am the person who is representing my client. I am the person that people could be pointing their fingers at. So please, Your Honours, understand I am speaking from my heart. And I will follow my conscience and my skills and professionalism to present as good, as best a case as I can. And the -- we are all part of this, and even though some of us come from thousands of miles away and are not in a position to know all the details, I think that we should still be able to have all the same body of information in order to arrive at the judgement. I'm going to -- I'm going to try to let you know what are some of the problems that we are facing with witnesses that are of Bosniak ethnic background, problems that arise from various attempts at obstruction by some intelligence services through the media. Your Honours, if the media published -- if you find that in some media outlets that such-and-such witnesses are giving evidence against or accusing Mladen Naletilic and then you get the names of protected witnesses. I am going to just hint at these matters now. It is not something that we should discuss now, but in due course and based on your decisions, I will ask an ex parte hearing where I will provide full details of this, and I will ask for your protection and assistance. So this is just to foreshadow something that is coming. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber will take note of what you have said during our deliberations on the time schedule of this trial. So having said that, I guess that's all. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 5.58 p.m.
